headings: List and define 30 key terms in the philosophy of AI.
List and provide clear explanations of 15 key concepts in the philosophy of AI.
Provide a salient description of the most critical issues within the philosophy of AI today.
Provide a list of resources relevant to the philosophy of AI.
Which universities currently have strong programs in the philosophy of AI?
Provide 15 discussion questions relevant to the content above.
introHeading: AI concepts: capability, understanding and responsibility
intro: Six original prompts lead from terminology and philosophical concepts to practical issues, reading resources, university study and discussion. Both model responses remain separate. Resource and university entries were checked for this editorial revision on November 26, 2026.
description: Explore AI capability, consciousness, ethics and study resources through six original prompts and twelve separately preserved model responses.

replacements.1.1.6: Unsupervised learning: methods that identify structure in data without supplied target labels. Designers still choose representations, objectives and evaluation methods; “unsupervised” does not mean free of human assumptions.
replacements.1.1.7: Reinforcement learning: learning a policy for choosing actions to obtain high expected reward. The reward is a specified signal and may fail to capture what people actually value.
replacements.1.1.12: Strong AI: in Searle’s philosophical usage, the claim that an appropriately programmed computer can literally possess a mind and understanding. Popular usage sometimes equates it with general capability, but that is a different claim.
replacements.1.1.13: Weak AI: in the philosophical contrast, treating computer programs as useful models or tools for studying minds without claiming that running the program constitutes a mind. This should be distinguished from narrow AI, which concerns the range of tasks performed.
replacements.1.1.14: Artificial general intelligence (AGI): broadly transferable competence across cognitive tasks. Definitions and thresholds vary; breadth of performance does not by itself settle consciousness or understanding.
replacements.1.1.23: Bias in AI: systematic tendencies arising from data, design, measurement or deployment. Statistical bias and unfair social outcomes are related but distinct senses; not every useful inductive bias is prejudice.
replacements.1.1.27: Human-in-the-loop: human participation in training, evaluation or operation. Meaningful oversight requires appropriate information, authority and time; mere presence does not guarantee control.
replacements.1.2.0: Artificial general intelligence (AGI): broadly transferable cognitive competence rather than a system limited to one defined task. There is no single agreed threshold, and the term does not entail consciousness.
replacements.1.2.3: Chinese Room argument: Searle’s challenge to the claim that executing a formal program is sufficient for understanding. It concerns the relation between syntax and semantics; critics dispute whether the understanding of the whole system is captured by the person manipulating symbols.
replacements.1.2.12: Consciousness: in the relevant phenomenal sense, subjective experience—there being something it is like to be the system. Responsiveness and wakefulness are related but distinct notions; behavior alone does not settle this question.
replacements.1.2.18: Machine ethics: inquiry into how artificial systems might choose or act in ways constrained by ethical considerations. The broader ethics of AI also examines the responsibilities of people and institutions that develop and deploy them.
replacements.1.2.25: Artificial empathy: systems that recognize emotional cues or produce responses perceived as empathetic. Simulating an empathetic response does not establish that the system shares anyone’s feelings.
replacements.2.1.1: Philosophical behaviorism: analyzes mental concepts in terms of behavior or dispositions to behave. It does not establish that machines necessarily lack understanding; rather, it raises the question of what behavioral criteria justify mental attribution.
replacements.2.1.9: Hard problem of consciousness: why and how physical or functional processes are accompanied by subjective experience. Posing this explanatory problem does not itself prove that computation can never support consciousness.
replacements.2.1.12: Singularity: a speculative discontinuity in technological development, often associated with rapidly accelerating or self-improving AI. It is distinct from merely exceeding human performance on particular tasks.
replacements.2.2.1: Artificial general intelligence (AGI): imagine competence that transfers across substantially different tasks, with flexible learning in unfamiliar settings. Whether and when a system meets that description depends on a stated definition and evidence; “distant future” is not a justified timetable.
replacements.2.2.4: Chinese Room argument: imagine a person following formal rules for producing Chinese responses without understanding Chinese. Searle uses this to argue that program execution alone is insufficient for understanding. The argument and replies to it concern more than whether a chatbot passes a test.
replacements.2.2.13: Machine ethics: studies whether and how machines can make ethically constrained decisions. Building in a rule or objective does not ensure alignment with all human values, especially when those values conflict.
replacements.2.2.15: Artificial consciousness debate: whether artificial systems can have subjective experience and what evidence would support that attribution. Being responsive to surroundings is insufficient as a definition of experience.
replacements.6.1.8: How do different degrees of machine autonomy change human oversight, employment and daily life? Which decisions should remain contestable by affected people?
replacements.6.2.3: Searle’s Chinese Room argument challenges the sufficiency of formal program execution for understanding. Which reply to that argument is strongest, and why?
replacements.6.2.9: What distinguishes explaining intelligent behavior from explaining subjective experience, and what evidence could bear on consciousness in artificial systems?
replacements.1.2.19: Moral Machine: an online study collecting people’s judgments about stylized autonomous-vehicle dilemmas. Reported preferences describe responses to scenarios; they do not establish which decisions are morally right.
replacements.1.2.27: Frame problem: originally, how to represent what remains unchanged when an action occurs without listing every unaffected fact. Broader uses concern relevance and efficient reasoning, but those should not erase the original problem.
replacements.1.2.28: Goodhart’s law: a statistical regularity can fail when used as a target for control. In AI, optimizing a proxy such as clicks can diverge from the intended goal, such as informed satisfaction.
replacements.1.1.17: Explainable AI (XAI): methods for making system behavior understandable to people. A plausible explanation may be incomplete or inaccurate; explanation must be checked against the system’s actual behavior.
replacements.1.1.21: Ontology in AI: an explicit representation of entities, categories and relations in a domain. Unlike philosophical ontology in general, a practical AI ontology may serve a limited modeling purpose without claiming to describe everything that exists.
replacements.2.1.4: Computational theory of mind: a family of views explaining cognition through computations over representations. The analogy with software is useful, but theories differ about representation, implementation and whether computation explains every aspect of mind.
replacements.2.2.2: Artificial narrow intelligence (ANI): competence restricted to a bounded task or domain, as illustrated by a chess-playing system. The boundary between narrow and general systems depends on breadth, transfer and the criteria used.
replacements.2.2.12: Explainable AI (XAI): methods that help people understand system behavior. An explanation earns trust only if it is faithful and useful; a persuasive story about a wrong output can instead increase misplaced confidence.
replacements.4.1.0: These resources offer different entry points: books for sustained arguments, journals for research, course materials for guided study, and public forums for developing debates. Publication or institutional affiliation does not establish that every claim is correct.
replacements.4.1.24: Online study alternative: MIT’s Social and Ethical Responsibilities of Computing materials. The original NYU/edX course attribution is not verified.
replacements.4.1.25: These open materials include case studies and teaching activities about responsible computing; they are not a promise of a currently enrolling degree or certificate.
replacements.4.2.3: The original title “Our Moral Obligation to Develop Artificial Intelligence Carefully,” attributed to Roman Yampolskiy, is unverified. For a documented alternative on artificial minds, see Artificial Minds by Stan Franklin.
replacements.4.2.5: Artificial Intelligence: A Guide for Thinking Humans by Melanie Mitchell. This corrects the original unverified title “A Mind Forged in Steel.”
replacements.4.2.14: LessWrong’s Nick Bostrom topic page: a collection of discussions, not the single article by Eliezer Yudkowsky described in the original list.
replacements.4.2.15: The Chinese Room Argument, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, by David Cole. This is an overview of Searle’s argument and replies, not an encyclopedia entry authored by Searle.
replacements.4.2.16: The original monkey-typing article attribution is unverified. For a more directly relevant overview, use Artificial Intelligence in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
replacements.4.2.17: The original Chalmers article title/link pairing is unverified. Read the consciousness discussion and bibliography in the Stanford Encyclopedia’s AI entry as a documented starting point.
replacements.4.2.20: Ex Machina (2015): fictional drama, useful for discussing manipulation, evidence of mind and power; it is not a documentary.
replacements.4.2.21: A.I. Artificial Intelligence: fictional drama, not a documentary. The original list’s 2016 date should not be treated as its release date.
replacements.5.1.0: The institutions below offer relevant research or teaching environments. This is a starting list rather than a comparative ranking. A research institute is not itself a degree program: check the awarding department, current courses, supervision and admissions separately.
replacements.5.1.41: Choose according to your question: consciousness and cognition, technical foundations, or ethics and governance. Check whether a relevant supervisor accepts students and whether the advertised route is a degree, short course or research affiliation.
replacements.5.2.0: Several routes connect philosophy with AI, including formal philosophy degrees, interdisciplinary teaching and research centres. The original blanket claim that dedicated programs do not exist is too strong; Cambridge, for example, lists an MPhil in Ethics of AI, Data and Algorithms.
replacements.5.2.1: Carnegie Mellon University: its philosophy department offers philosophy and logic-and-computation majors, among others, with applications to AI and cognitive science. These are distinct from its technical AI degree.
replacements.5.2.5: New York University: Minds, Brains, and Machines connects research on human and machine intelligence. Consult the relevant degree catalog separately; this does not validate the original “Philosophy and Neural Sciences” program description.
replacements.5.2.6: University of California, Berkeley: the Center for Human-Compatible Artificial Intelligence researches beneficial AI across technical and policy questions. It is a research centre within computer science, not a standalone philosophy degree.
replacements.5.2.7: Australian National University: the Master of Applied Cybernetics addresses responsible technological systems. It is offered by the School of Cybernetics; the original mental-health-institute MPhil in AI and Society claim is unsupported.
replacements.5.1.4: Relevant route: Stanford’s HAI offers interdisciplinary research, education and policy concerning human-centered AI.
replacements.5.1.7: Relevant route: MIT’s SERC offers social and ethical responsibilities of computing through research and teaching.
replacements.5.1.10: Relevant route: Harvard’s Berkman Klein Center offers public inquiry into how AI affects human meaning and society.
replacements.5.1.13: Relevant route: Toronto’s Schwartz Reisman Institute offers interdisciplinary research on the social impacts of advanced technologies.
replacements.5.1.17: Relevant route: Oxford’s Institute for Ethics in AI offers philosophically grounded research on AI ethics, safety and governance.
replacements.5.1.20: Relevant route: Cambridge’s Leverhulme Centre offers an MPhil in Ethics of AI, Data and Algorithms.
replacements.5.1.23: Relevant route: Edinburgh’s Centre for Technomoral Futures offers research on ethical implications of AI and data-driven technologies.
replacements.5.1.26: Relevant route: ETH AI Ethics Policy network offers connections among researchers and practitioners in AI ethics and policy.
replacements.5.1.30: Relevant route: Tsinghua’s Institute for AI International Governance offers research on international AI governance.
replacements.5.1.33: Relevant route: NUS AI Institute offers AI governance and policy research; this corrects the original centre attribution.
replacements.5.1.37: Relevant route: UNSW AI Institute offers an interdisciplinary AI research environment; applicants should separately establish which philosophy or ethics supervision is available.
replacements.5.1.40: Relevant route: ANU School of Cybernetics offers the Master of Applied Cybernetics, a route into responsible technological systems rather than a degree titled philosophy of AI.
replacements.5.2.2: Relevant route: Oxford’s Institute for Ethics in AI offers philosophically grounded research on AI ethics, safety and governance.
replacements.5.2.3: Relevant route: Stanford’s HAI offers interdisciplinary research, education and policy concerning human-centered AI.
replacements.5.2.4: Relevant route: MIT’s SERC offers social and ethical responsibilities of computing through research and teaching.
replacements.3.1.9: Implications: audit outcomes using explicit fairness criteria and affected groups. Different criteria can conflict; transparency helps expose tradeoffs but does not ensure fairness.
replacements.3.1.20: Issue: automating tasks can displace workers, change job content or create complementary work. The scale and distribution depend on deployment, demand and institutions; displacement is a risk rather than a uniform forecast.
replacements.3.1.26: Issue: linking and analyzing personal data can expose sensitive patterns or enable intrusive decisions. More data does not automatically mean more accurate inference; mistaken inferences can also harm privacy and autonomy.
replacements.3.1.29: Issue: AI raises questions about who bears responsibility, which rights should apply and how decisions can be challenged. Answers depend on jurisdiction and use; this philosophical overview does not assess the adequacy of every current legal system.
replacements.3.2.4: Explainable AI (XAI): explanations can help people identify errors and challenge decisions. Safety also requires performance evidence, controls and accountability; intelligibility alone is insufficient.
replacements.3.2.7: Moral Machine: survey scenarios reveal differing preferences about vehicle dilemmas. Those responses raise questions about whose preferences should influence design; popularity does not establish a morally justified rule.
replacements.6.2.10: The Moral Machine survey explores judgments about stylized vehicle dilemmas. What can such preferences tell us, and why might ethical design also require principles that a majority rejects?
replacements.4.1.20: AI for Everyone, taught by Andrew Ng: a nontechnical introduction including societal implications.
replacements.4.1.34: AI Alignment Podcast, Future of Life Institute.
replacements.4.1.6: Artificial Intelligence: A Guide for Thinking Humans by Melanie Mitchell.
replacements.4.1.10: Philosophy and Theory of Artificial Intelligence, edited by Vincent C. Müller.
replacements.4.1.22: Philosophical Issues in Brain Science, MIT OpenCourseWare (Spring 2009 materials), replaces the original imprecise course title.

reviewDecisions: Source read in indexed ranges 1–100,101–200,201–334 (including duplicated navigation and introductory quotations). Current article read in character ranges 0–20000 and 20000–39198.
1: retain both thirty-term inventories; repair strong/weak AI versus breadth, consciousness, proxy optimization, frame problem, empathy and oversight.
2: retain two fifteen-concept explanations; correct behaviorism, computation, consciousness, AGI timetable and explainability.

3: retained both issue structures; replaced fairness guarantees, uniform employment forecasts, data-volume certainty and blanket legal adequacy claims; distinguished survey preference from moral justification.
4: retained all categories and item positions; verified or explicitly qualified questionable resource attributions, supplied documented alternatives, and separated documentary from fiction.
5: retain all institutions and geographic order; cite official routes and distinguish research institutes from degrees; replace unsupported ANU/NYU descriptions.
6: retain both fifteen-question sets; revise questions dependent on erroneous concepts.
